title: How to Maximize Your Charts' Impact
author: Impactful Speaking
summary: A presentation coach argues that technical accuracy is not the same as communicating meaning, using the example of a box plot that a trained eye reads instantly and a general audience sees only as an unlabeled rectangle. Drawing an analogy to how a doctor or mechanic notices details a layperson misses, the piece argues that experts habitually describe what they see rather than explain what it means, leaving audiences with accurate facts but no usable conclusion. It distinguishes between academic and business contexts: researchers can present findings and let peers draw their own conclusions, but executives and clients who hired an expert expect that person to have already done the interpretive work and to arrive with a recommendation. The author also warns against over-detailing a presentation to look more rigorous, since audiences who can't follow ten charts often conclude the presenter is the problem. The piece closes by framing a clear recommendation, stated with appropriate uncertainty, as part of the responsibility that comes with being the expert in the room.
points: The core failure mode identified is technically accurate but meaningless delivery: describing a box plot's median and spread precisely while the audience only sees a rectangle with lines coming out of it.

Academic and business audiences operate under different contracts -- researchers can present findings without a firm recommendation, but executives and clients expect the expert to have already done the interpretive work.
Adding more charts to appear rigorous backfires: audiences who can't follow ten charts start doubting the presenter rather than being reassured by the apparent thoroughness.

The author argues withholding a recommendation to avoid being wrong is itself a failure of expertise, since the audience may then miss a pattern that was obvious to the person who understood the data.
quotes: I know they are better at showing actual data than plain averages. And data scientists may see the median, the spread, the unusual values, and the difference between two groups. But other people might only see a rectangle with lines coming out of it.
Expertise changes the way we look at information. We see things others can't and understand nuances others don't.
The audience does not have access to that trained eye. They only have access to the slide and to our explanation.
These people invited an expert because they need help interpreting something outside their own field. Their time is limited. They may also need to make a decision soon after the presentation.
Ten charts don't make a slide more complete; it makes it more confusing. Good preparation involves choosing what the audience needs now and keeping the rest available for questions.
Expertise brings a responsibility to interpret. That responsibility includes stating our level of confidence and acknowledging the limits of the available information.
